recommendations.title_changes: Keep current — 'Why You're Doing It Wrong' is a strong contrarian hook absent from the SERP. - Add an FAQ section before the closing CTA.

- 5–7 concrete benefits with brief examples — trust, conflict resolution, learning speed, emotional safety, decision quality (canonical SERP element across CCL/HelpGuide/Asana).
- 2–3 short dialogue examples showing fake vs real listening (Asana ranks specifically for 'examples' modifier — clear gap).

pages.title: Types of Listening: The Improv Framework for Understanding How We Hear
pages.description: There aren't just 'good' and 'bad' listening. Improv identifies specific listening modes — and teaches when each one helps and when it kills the conversation.

research.primary_intent: informational — definitional / educational with strong taxonomy expectation
user_questions: What are the 4 types of listening?
What are the 7 types of listening?
What's the difference between hearing and listening?
What is empathic listening?
What is critical listening?
What's the most important type of listening?
research.search_volume_data: Frontmatter (article-author estimates): 'types of listening' = 800/mo, 'types of listening skills' = 1200/mo, 'listening styles' = 300/mo. Combined ~2300/mo.
competitor_titles: 9 Types Of Listening (BetterUp)
Listening Style (UW Local Government Extension)
Types of Listening — Fundamentals of Public Speaking (OpenFL Pressbooks)
The Main Types and Levels of Listening (The Right Questions)
12 Types of Listening (The Knowledge Academy)
The 5 types of listening (Tammy Lenski)
Active listening (Wikipedia)
All types of listening (ChangingMinds)
The 3 Levels of Listening (Matt Russell / Medium)
Types of Listening (SkillsYouNeed)
research.gap_analysis: Article's '3 attention modes' (broadcast, evaluative, receptive) is a sharp reframe — but it bypasses the canonical taxonomy (informational, empathetic, comprehensive, critical, discriminative, appreciative, active) that nearly every top-10 result enumerates. Readers searching 'types of listening' arrive expecting that list, and our article essentially refuses to provide it. This is a real intent mismatch: our deeper insight (modes-not-types) loses the click before it can deliver value. Other gaps: no definition snippet, no 'hearing vs listening' clarifier (PAA), no FAQ.
research.notes: SERP features: AI Overview likely. Listicle pattern dominates (3, 5, 9, 12). Educational/academic authority (Pressbooks, UW, ChangingMinds, SkillsYouNeed). Score 3 because the article addresses the right topic but with a contrarian framing that bypasses the canonical taxonomy readers arrive expecting. The 3-modes insight is sharp but currently functions as a replacement for the standard list rather than a layer above it — and at this volume, that's a costly intent mismatch.

recommendations.title_changes: Recommended shift: meet searcher expectation while preserving the differentiator. e.g. 'Types of Listening: The 7 Canonical Types and 3 Attention Modes That Matter More'. Trades a contrarian-only stance for a both/and structure.
recommendations.structural_changes:
- Add a TL;DR / definition box at the very top.
- Add a 'Canonical types of listening' enumeration section first — the 7 traditional types (informational, empathetic, comprehensive, critical, discriminative, appreciative, active). This satisfies the searcher expectation that's currently being missed.
- THEN layer the 3 attention modes (broadcast / evaluative / receptive) as the deeper framework — 'these types tell you WHAT you might be doing; the modes explain what your attention is actually DOING'.
- Add a 'Hearing vs listening' clarifier (PAA gap).
- Add an FAQ section before the closing.
recommendations.content_additions:
- Definition snippet (PAA + featured-snippet capture).
- Canonical types enumeration with brief 1-line each — provides the list readers came for.
- Layered framework explanation: how the 3 modes underlie the 7 types (e.g. critical listening is evaluative mode applied to content; empathic is receptive mode applied to emotion).
- 'Hearing vs listening' distinction (PAA).
- FAQ: 'What are the 4 types of listening?', 'What are the 7 types?', 'What's the difference between hearing and listening?', 'Which type is most important?', 'What's empathic listening?'.
recommendations.content_removals: - The current opening that essentially dismisses canonical taxonomies as 'technically correct and practically useless' is too combative when the searcher came specifically for that taxonomy. Soften the framing: acknowledge the canonical types as useful labels, then offer the modes as the practical layer underneath.

pages.title: What Is Improv? (It's Not What You Think)
pages.description: Improv isn't comedy — it's the art of building shared reality in real time with no script. Here's what actually happens on stage and why it matters.

research.primary_intent: informational — definitional with curious-newcomer audience
user_questions: What is the purpose of improv?
What are the rules of improv?
What's the difference between improv and improvisation?
Who invented improv?
What are the types of improv?
Is improv only comedy?
research.search_volume_data: Frontmatter (article-author estimates): 'what is improv' = 1600/mo, 'what is improvisation' = 800/mo. Combined ~2400/mo. Note: this is one of only two bridges with status='validated' in frontmatter (most are 'draft') — content quality has already been signed off.
competitor_titles: Improv, explained (University of Chicago News)
Improvisational theatre (Wikipedia)
What is Improv? (Covert Theatre)
What is Improv? Understanding Improv Acting, Theater and Improvisation (Coronation Theater)
What Is Improv? A Beginner's Guide (Change Through Play)
What in the World is Improv? (Drama Kids)
WHAT IS IMPROV (Improvibe)
IMPROVISATION Definition & Meaning (Merriam-Webster)
If You're Good at Improv, You're Going to be Good at Life (NTPA)
Improv group post (Facebook)
research.gap_analysis: Article's 'improv = reality construction, not comedy' frame is genuinely fresh — Wikipedia and most theater-school competitors lead with 'improv comedy where actors make up scenes', and our article reframes the question to a deeper definition. Strong differentiator. Gaps: no shortform-vs-longform distinction (universal SERP element from UChicago and Wikipedia); no brief history (where it came from — commedia dell'arte → Spolin → Compass/Second City — every reference SERP includes this); no 'applied improv' mention (classrooms, business, therapy use); no FAQ; no definition snippet formatted for featured-snippet capture.
research.notes: SERP features: AI Overview likely; UChicago + Wikipedia + Merriam-Webster anchor as reference authority. Rest is theater-school cluster (Covert, Coronation, Drama Kids, NTPA) plus social (Facebook). Lower competitive intensity than other definitional queries — the 'what is X' format here mostly serves curious newcomers, not researchers. Score 4 because the article addresses dominant intent with a sharper conceptual frame than any competitor and is the only validated-status article in our bridge set, but is missing canonical structural elements (shortform/longform, history, applied improv, FAQ) that newcomers expect from a definitional page.

recommendations.title_changes: Keep current — '(It's Not What You Think)' is sticky and absent from competitor titles. No change recommended.
recommendations.structural_changes:
- Add a TL;DR / definition box at the very top (PAA + featured-snippet capture for 'what is improv').
- Add a 'Shortform vs longform' brief subsection — universal SERP element (UChicago, Wikipedia both reference this distinction).
- Add a 'Where improv came from' callout with a 3-sentence history (commedia dell'arte → Spolin → Second City → present) and a link to /improv-theory for depth.
- Add an 'Applied improv: classrooms, business, therapy' brief mention — referenced in nearly every authority result.
- Add an FAQ section before the closing.
recommendations.content_additions:
- Definition snippet: 'Improv is the art of building shared reality in real time…' formatted as a 2–3 sentence direct answer (PAA).
- Shortform vs longform: brief explanation + an example of each (Whose Line for shortform, Harold for longform).
- Compressed history with link to /improv-theory.
- Applied improv: 1–2 sentences about its use in education, business communication training, therapy.
- FAQ: 'What's the purpose of improv?', 'Who invented it?', 'What's the difference between improv and improvisation?', 'Is improv only comedy?', 'What are the rules?', 'How do I get started?'.
recommendations.content_removals: - Article is well-written and already validated. Minor: trim the opening 'most people picture' framing if needed once the TL;DR exists, since the contrarian setup should land in the first ~60 words rather than the first ~200.
